title: Cervical Referred Pain
purpose: Screen for true and referred visceral pain presenting as neck and shoulder pain, so serious pathology can be referred out.
structure: Viscera sharing segmental innervation with the cervical spine: cardiopulmonary tract (incl. Pancoast tumour mimicking C8 radiculopathy / ulnar entrapment), digestive organs irritating the diaphragm (C3-C5), and the locomotor tract (systemic inflammatory disease).
procedure: History screening. Pulmonary: smoking, dyspnoea, wheezing, prolonged cough, sputum, asthma/emphysema/pneumonia/TB. Cardiovascular: heart trouble, chest pain or pressure, palpitations, smoking, hypertension, dyspnoea incl. nocturnal, limb swelling, family history, cholesterol. Digestive: dysphagia, nausea/heartburn, vomiting, food intolerance, constipation, diarrhoea, stool colour, rectal bleeding, jaundice, liver/gallbladder history. Locomotor: pain, swelling or restriction in other joints. Start general and dig deeper when positive.
positive: A pattern suggesting visceral pain: symptoms unrelated to position or movement, present at rest or waking the patient at night; diffuse, dull, poorly localised, possibly cramping; related to organ function (eating, bowel/bladder); insidious onset without trauma; constitutional signs (fever, chills, nausea, unexplained weight loss, malaise, bleeding >1-2 weeks); risk from age, gender, occupation, ethnicity, past conditions.

accuracy.source: n/a (screening overview). References: Sikandar & Dickenson 2012; Boissonnault & Bass 1990 parts I and II

notes: Visceral pain is often accompanied by motor and autonomic reflexes (pallor, sweating, nausea, GI disturbance, changes in temperature, blood pressure, heart rate) and strong affective responses. The page's reference list is printed twice. Companion pages: referred pain thoracic spine, referred pain lumbar spine.

title: Extension Rotation Test
purpose: Pre-manipulative test for vertebrobasilar insufficiency (VBI) by compressing the vertebral artery.
structure: Vertebral artery (transverse foramina C6-C1, tethered at C2, C1 and the atlanto-occipital membrane); hindbrain blood supply.
procedure: Patient supine with the head beyond the edge of the table. Support the head, rotate it submaximally to one side and bring it into extension. Hold 30 seconds; talk to the patient or have them count to 20 to detect speech changes, and watch the eyes for nystagmus. The artery on the side of rotation is the one being tested (it must compensate for the compromised contralateral flow).
positive: Any typical sign or symptom of VBI (listed in an overview table on the page); all are absolute contraindications to cervical manipulation and need urgent referral.

accuracy.source: Hutting et al. 2013 systematic review (Man Ther)

notes: Source: a surplus value of pre-manipulative tests seems unlikely; knowledge of pathophysiology, risk factors and the classic vascular presentation matters more. Recommends screening cranial nerves VIII-XII for cervical artery dysfunction. ⚠ The VBI signs/symptoms table referred to on the page is an image not present in the API text. Rivett et al. 2005 also listed.

title: Sharp Purser Test
purpose: Pre-manipulative screen for upper cervical instability: integrity of the transverse ligament of the atlas.
structure: Transverse ligament of the atlas (keeps the dens of the axis against the anterior arch of C1); atlantodens interval.
procedure: Patient sitting, neck relaxed and semi-flexed (this may already produce cord symptoms). Index finger of one hand on the spinous process of C2, the other hand on the forehead. Press the forehead backwards and look for posterior sliding of the head relative to the axis.
positive: Excessive motion, sliding or a clunk felt or heard; or reduction of cord-compression symptoms present in flexion when the occiput and atlas are translated posteriorly (the anterior subluxation is reduced).

accuracy.source: Hutting et al. 2013 systematic review (Phys Ther); reliability kappa 0.06-0.67; Mansfield et al. 2020 also listed

notes: Source: weak clinical value. Upper cervical instability prevalence 0.6% (Beck 2004); associated with rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, trauma, Down syndrome, Marfan. Page writes the figures as decimals (0.19-0.69, 0.71-0.98).

title: Transverse Ligament Test
purpose: Anterior shear test for transverse ligament integrity (upper cervical instability).
procedure: Mintken et al. 2008 description: patient supine, head on a pillow in neutral. Cup the occiput in the palms with fingers 3-5, both index fingers in the space between the occiput and the C2 spinous process over the neural arch of the atlas. Lift the head and C1 together anteriorly, keeping the head neutral; gravity fixates the rest of the neck.
positive: Symptoms other than local pain or soreness: a lump in the throat, or signs and symptoms of spinal cord compression.

accuracy.source: Hutting et al. 2013 systematic review (Phys Ther)

notes: Source: moderate clinical value as a pre-manipulative screen. Companion tests: Sharp-Purser, upper cervical flexion, alar ligament stress, lateral shear.

title: Upper Cervical Flexion Test
purpose: Provocation test for transverse ligament tear (upper cervical instability).
structure: Transverse ligament; dens of C2 tilting backwards against the dura / spinal cord during the upper cervical nod.
procedure: Patient supine; stand at the head of the bench. Fixate C3 with a key grip in a ventrocranial direction; the other hand high on the occiput, the forehead fixated by your shoulder or chest. Perform a gentle upper cervical flexion (nod).
positive: Symptoms of dural compression (diffuse pain over several upper-back and head segments) or of spinal cord compression.

accuracy.source: none; no diagnostic accuracy studies. Reliability: Cattrysse et al. 1997, intra-rater -0.27 to 1, inter-rater kappa 0.64-1

notes: Source: questionable clinical value. The page explains why C3 (not C2, as in most literature) is fixated: fixating C2 would stop the dens from tilting backwards. ⚠ The page header reads 'Valgus Stress Test for MCL Injuries' (copy error from a knee page); the body is the upper cervical flexion test.

title: Alar Ligament Stress Test
purpose: Pre-manipulative screen for alar ligament insufficiency (upper cervical instability).
structure: Alar ligaments limiting side-bending and rotation between occiput, atlas and axis.
procedure: Mintken et al. 2008 description: patient supine. Grip and stabilise the spinous process of C2, side-bend the head and atlas and assess range and end-feel; repeat both sides. Then repeat with rotation of head and atlas on the axis.
positive: Excessive range compared with the other side or a soft end-feel. Intact ligament: little or no side-bending to the opposite side, capsular end-feel.

accuracy.source: Hutting et al. 2013 systematic review (Phys Ther); Harry Von P et al. 2019 also listed

notes: Source: moderate clinical value as a pre-manipulative screen.

title: Lateral Shear Test
purpose: Lateral displacement test for upper cervical instability (page header: alar ligament rupture; body text: transverse ligament integrity).
structure: Atlanto-axial segment (C1 on C2); lateral translation.
procedure: Patient supine; stand at the head of the bench. Index finger of one hand dorsolaterally against the arch of C2; the other hand holds the occiput and C1 from the opposite lateral side. Bring the upper cervical spine into slight flexion (moves the dens posteriorly from the anterior arch), approximate both hands to take up soft-tissue slack and judge the amount of movement and end-feel. Repeat on the other side.
positive: Lateral translation between the segments, which is usually absent in healthy subjects.

accuracy.source: none; reliability only: Cattrysse et al. 1997, intra-rater kappa 0.09-0.67, inter-rater -0.64 to 0.45

notes: Source: weak clinical value. ⚠ Header says 'Alar Ligament Rupture' while the text says 'we are testing the left transverse ligament'. ⚠ The only listed reference is the 2017 BPPV clinical practice guideline (Bhattacharyya et al.), unrelated to the test; Cattrysse 1997 is cited in the text but not listed.

title: Spurling’s Test
purpose: Provocation test for cervical radicular syndrome by narrowing the intervertebral foramen.
procedure: Most provocative version (Anekstein): neck extension, lateral bending to the affected side, then axial compression. Build up gradually: start with extension and lateral bending only, add axial compression only if symptoms are not reproduced.
positive: Reproduction of radiating arm pain or paraesthesia; distal pain distribution distinguishes radiculopathy from cervical spondylosis (proximal neck pain only).

accuracy.source: Wainner et al. 2003 (Spine); Anekstein et al. (text 2011, reference 2012) compared six modifications

notes: Source: moderate clinical value (low sensitivity, high specificity). ⚠ The cluster-of-Wainner page gives Spurling A specificity 86% while this page gives 83% for the same Wainner 2003 source. ⚠ Anekstein cited as 2011 in text, 2012 in the reference list.

title: Cervical Distraction Test
purpose: Symptom-relief test for cervical radicular syndrome (traction/distraction test).
procedure: Patient supine; apply longitudinal traction with the fingers hooked under the occiput. Only meaningful if the patient currently has shooting pain or paraesthesia down the arm.
positive: Reduction of the familiar arm pain.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 2007 systematic review (Eur Spine J), spelled 'Rubenstein' on the page; Hanney et al. 2014 (reliability) also listed

notes: Source: moderate clinical value to confirm cervical radicular syndrome. One of the four tests in the cluster of Wainner.

title: Cluster of Wainner
purpose: Four-test cluster (Wainner et al. 2003) to confirm cervical radicular syndrome.
procedure: (1) ULTT1: supine, depress the shoulder, abduct 110 degrees, external rotation, supinate the forearm, extend wrist and fingers, slowly extend the elbow; confirm neural tension by releasing elbow tension and adding contralateral lateral flexion. (2) Cervical rotation to the affected side measured with an inclinometer or CROM device. (3) Traction/distraction test: supine, longitudinal traction under the occiput. (4) Spurling test A: sitting, lateral flexion to the affected side with about 7 kg overpressure.
positive: (1) familiar shooting pain or tingling reproduced; (2) rotation less than 60 degrees (healthy about 80 degrees); (3) familiar arm pain reduced; (4) familiar arm pain increased. 3 of 4 or 4 of 4 positive confirms.

accuracy.sensitivity: item values: ULTT1 97%; rotation <60 degrees 89%; distraction 44%; Spurling A 50%
accuracy.specificity: item values: ULTT1 22%; rotation 49%; distraction 90%; Spurling A 86%

notes: Source: only moderate clinical value because of the huge confidence interval (small sample) and a hospital setting that may not transfer to primary care. ⚠ Spurling A specificity is given as 86% here but 83% on the Spurling's test page.

title: Valsalva Maneuver
purpose: Provocation test for cervical radicular syndrome by raising intraspinal pressure.
procedure: Patient sitting takes a deep breath and holds it while attempting to exhale against the closed airway for 2-3 seconds with gradually increasing force (or blow against the back of the hand, bear down, or equalise ear pressure).
positive: Reproduction of arm pain or paraesthesia.
notes: Source: raises post-test probability but weak as a stand-alone test.

title: Shoulder Abduction Sign
purpose: Shoulder abduction relief test: do the arm symptoms stem from cervical root pathology?
structure: Cervical nerve root (reduced tension of the root with the arm abducted).
procedure: Patient sitting with current symptoms; ask the patient to abduct the affected arm and rest the hand on top of the head.

accuracy.source: Rubinstein et al. 2006 systematic review as cited in text; the only listed reference is Wainner et al. 2003

notes: Source: clinical utility at least questionable; pooling impossible because of heterogeneity. ⚠ Rubinstein 2006 is cited in the text but not in the reference list.
